doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Staying with Marsalis rather than leading his own band
summary: Asked about young players leading bands sooner, Gordon says he chose to keep growing in Marsalis's septet since 1989 rather than start a solo career.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Is there a difference in your opinion of how young jazz players make their mark in today’s music than twenty-five years ago?
How they make their mark. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Well let me put it this way. Some people have said that the young musicians get their own bands a lot sooner than some of the fellas like Sweets Edison and Al Grey and all those guys. Does that seem to be true in your case?

In our generation I think that does happen. In my case I think that I waited a little while, I played with Wynton for almost, since ’89, eleven, going on twelve years and I’ve had an association with him, I still do. But in terms of acting as a leader there was a time someone had come to me, heard me on a couple of gigs with Wynton and said, “You know you should record a record.” And at that time I felt that I was still in a period or in a stage in my growth where I just wasn’t ready to do that. It was like a choice between leave the band and start a solo career or stay in the band and continue to develop at the pace. And once I kind of fit — because the first year and a half, almost two years I was in the band I didn’t get a chance to play a lot because I was the seventh member to join the septet and there was not a lot of music written. And then I had to get my stuff together because when I met Wynton, when I was in college, it was kind of like big fish in a small pond. And then when I got a chance to hear them play it was like oh — this is what’s happening, you know a cast of better playing. I wasn’t exposed to what was going on on the jazz scene. I heard about it but I got a chance to hear it firsthand with one of the most influential young musicians. And so when I was offered that opportunity I said oh, this is great, but I said I can break away now and attempt it, but I just felt that what was happening with me then, it was a much greater thing for me. But as a whole I believe that in our generation a lot of the guys are starting bands earlier, whereas in the generations that included Sweets Edison, folks like Al Grey and those musicians of that caliber, I think it was great to be a part of a great band or a great situation where you were in the band with all those great musicians. And they had great leaders. And it’s hard to — in any era really — to keep a band together for several reasons. A reason can be money. A reason can be mainly you have guys that become great players, great individual players. And they want to be band leaders. All the great players are not necessarily great band leaders, but the thing is if everyone was to become a great player then you never really would have a band. A band like the John Coltrane Quartet, you know they stayed together. Even Miles, he went through several bands but guys, you think about someone like Harry Carney that stayed with Duke forty years, his whole professional music career was with Duke Ellington’s band. And I guess he felt, as I did for a great period of time, that I was with Wynton Marsalis. This is a great musical situation.
Yeah. This is where I belong.

The growth that takes place, I can go out and become a solo musician and try to become a star but you know musically you just have to ask yourself sometimes, what are you going to be, what is going to give you the greatest gratification? The money that you’re going to © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
